meta.note: Plain-language explanations for readers who are new to the terms. They are summaries, not the legal definitions: the defining paragraph in the instrument named under 'See' governs.

terms.def: A company registered with RBI under Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act whose main business is lending, investing in securities, leasing or similar financial activity, but which is not a bank.
The wider term used in s.45-I of the RBI Act for a financial institution that is not a bank. An NBFC is an NBFI that is a company.

RBI's framework that places NBFCs in layers (Base, Middle, Upper and Top) by size, activity and risk. The rules get stricter as you go up, and each layer also follows the rules of the layers below it.
The lowest SBR layer: mainly non-deposit-taking NBFCs below ₹1,000 crore of assets, plus some types (such as P2P platforms, Account Aggregators and NOFHCs) that always stay here. Lightest regulation.
The SBR layer for larger non-deposit-taking NBFCs (₹1,000 crore of assets or more) and for all deposit-taking NBFCs, HFCs, IFCs, IDF-NBFCs, CICs and SPDs that are not in the Upper Layer.

The SBR layer for the largest NBFCs: since 24-06-2026, those with assets of ₹1,00,000 crore or more, identified by RBI each year. They face bank-like rules such as Common Equity Tier 1 capital and a listing requirement.
An SBR layer that is kept empty. RBI can move an Upper Layer NBFC into it if it sees a substantial increase in systemic risk.
An NBFC whose main business is financing housing. It is registered under s.29A of the NHB Act, regulated by RBI and inspected by NHB. HFCs sit in the Middle or Upper Layer.
The statutory body under the NHB Act, 1987 that supervises (inspects) HFCs and handles their complaints, while RBI makes the rules for them.
An NBFC allowed by RBI to accept public deposits. It is always at least in the Middle Layer and must follow the Public Deposits Directions.
An NBFC that does not accept public deposits.
The general NBFC category for companies that lend and/or invest. Most lending NBFCs are ICCs.
An NBFC that holds most of its assets as microfinance loans, i.e. collateral-free loans to low-income households.
An NBFC that deploys most of its assets in infrastructure loans.
An NBFC set up to refinance infrastructure projects, mainly through long-term debt.
An NBFC whose business is holding investments in its group companies, not lending to outsiders. Excluded from many lending Directions.
An NBFC whose main business is guaranteeing mortgage loans.
An NBFC that runs an online platform matching individual lenders and borrowers. It may not lend from its own balance sheet. Always in the Base Layer.
An NBFC that moves a customer's financial data between institutions with the customer's consent. Always in the Base Layer.
A holding company through which a promoter group holds a bank or other financial entities. Always in the Base Layer.
An NBFC authorised by RBI to deal in government securities as a primary dealer.
The registration RBI grants under s.45-IA of the RBI Act (or s.29A of the NHB Act for HFCs) that allows a company to carry on NBFC business. RBI can cancel it.
Broadly, paid-up capital and free reserves less losses, intangibles and certain investments in group companies. NBFCs must hold a minimum NOF to be registered.
Capital as a percentage of risk-weighted assets; the main measure of whether an NBFC has enough capital for the risks it carries.
A loan whose interest or principal is overdue beyond the set period (90 days for most NBFC loans). It must be classified and provided for under the prudential norms.

terms.full: Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning
terms.def: The prudential rules on when income may be booked, how loans are classified (standard, NPA and so on) and how much must be set aside as provisions.
An early-warning label for a loan that is overdue but not yet an NPA (SMA-0, SMA-1, SMA-2 by days overdue).
A forward-looking way of providing for loan losses (as under Ind AS 109), based on the chance and size of future default.
The loan amount as a percentage of the value of the security, e.g. the gold pledged. RBI caps it for some loans.
The rules for identifying and verifying customers and monitoring their accounts to prevent money laundering and terrorist financing.
The central database of customers' KYC records. Lenders upload KYC data to it and can fetch existing records when onboarding a customer.
The income-tax identity number. Lenders must obtain the PAN, or Form 60 if the customer has none, when opening an account-based relationship.
A declaration given by a person who does not have a PAN, accepted in place of the PAN for KYC.
The anti-money-laundering law. NBFCs are reporting entities under it and must report certain transactions to FIU-IND.
The government body that receives cash and suspicious transaction reports from reporting entities under the PMLA.
A report to FIU-IND of a transaction that appears linked to money laundering or other crime.
A report to FIU-IND of cash transactions above the set threshold.

A senior independent officer inside a covered NBFC who must review complaints that the NBFC has partly or wholly rejected before the customer is told the final answer. HFCs, CICs, NBFC-IFCs and IDF-NBFCs are outside the 2026 Directions.
RBI's free complaint scheme for customers of regulated entities, including covered NBFCs, when the entity has not resolved the complaint.
A short standard sheet given to a borrower before the loan, showing the annual percentage rate, all charges and the repayment schedule.
The all-in yearly cost of a loan, including interest and fees, shown in the Key Fact Statement.
An agent of a lender that carries out functions such as sourcing customers, underwriting support or recovery in digital lending.
A mobile or web app, of the lender or its LSP, through which digital loans are offered.
A promise by a third party (such as an LSP) to cover a lender's losses on a loan portfolio up to a limit. RBI caps it and sets conditions.
Pooling loans and selling them to a special purpose entity, which pays for them by issuing notes (PTCs) to investors who are repaid from the loans' cash flows.
A separate trust or company set up only to buy a pool of loans in a securitisation and issue securitisation notes against it, so the assets are kept apart from the originator's own risks.
The usual form of securitisation note in India: investors receive the payments collected on the underlying loans, passed through by the SPE.
The lender that made the loans and transfers them to the SPE in a securitisation.
The share of a securitised pool that the originator must keep, so it keeps 'skin in the game'.
The minimum time a lender must hold a loan before it can securitise or transfer it.
Selling loans directly to another lender without an SPE or notes. It falls under the Transfer of Loan Exposures Directions, not the Securitisation Directions.
Held electronically in a depository account (NSDL or CDSL) instead of as a paper certificate.
The amount a single investor puts into securitisation notes. The minimum is ₹1 crore, and from 01-04-2027 it also applies at every transfer.

terms.full: Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India
terms.def: The central registry where security interests must be registered. Under SARFAESI s.26D a lender cannot enforce without registration.

terms.full: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002
terms.def: The law that lets notified secured lenders enforce security (e.g. take possession of the property) without going to court, above set loan sizes.
The insolvency law. CIRP under it is the process for resolving a company in default.
The foreign-exchange law. Foreign borrowing and lending by NBFCs is governed by regulations made under it.
Borrowing in foreign currency or rupees from lenders outside India. Since 16-02-2026 governed by the FEMA (Borrowing and Lending) Regulations as amended.

terms.full: Securities and Exchange Board of India
terms.def: The securities regulator. Listed NBFCs and public offers of securities (including securitisation notes) also follow SEBI rules.
aka: securities and exchange board of india

terms.def: The law under which lenders must report borrower data to credit bureaus (credit information companies).
The law for payment systems such as prepaid instruments and payment aggregators.
A wallet or card loaded with money in advance, regulated under the PSS Act.
The data-protection law that governs how lenders collect and use customers' personal data.
Loans for office, retail, hotel and similar property whose repayment depends mainly on the property's income or sale.
Managing the mismatch between when an NBFC's assets mature and when its liabilities fall due.
High-quality liquid assets held against expected net cash outflows over 30 days of stress. It applies to larger NBFCs.
Assets such as government securities that can quickly be turned into cash, counted for the LCR.
A Board-approved internal assessment of how much capital the NBFC needs for all its risks. Required for Middle and Upper Layer NBFCs.
RBI's framework that restricts an NBFC's activities when capital, asset quality or other measures breach set thresholds.
The senior officer responsible for the NBFC's compliance function, required for Middle and Upper Layer NBFCs.
An internal audit approach that focuses effort on the highest-risk areas, required for larger NBFCs.
A bank and an NBFC jointly lending to a borrower under a prior agreement, sharing the loan in agreed proportions.
A payment made through digital banking channels such as internet or mobile banking, UPI or cards.
A bank so large and connected that RBI applies extra capital requirements to it.
Development finance institutions such as NABARD, SIDBI, EXIM Bank and NHB, regulated by RBI under their own Directions.
A bank licensed to serve small borrowers and businesses, with its own RBI Directions.
